# A New Old Play

### Key Points
- **Overview**: *A New Old Play* is a 2021 Chinese drama film directed by Qiu Jiongjiong, blending elements of fiction, historical drama, and experimental theater. It follows the life of a Sichuan opera performer against the backdrop of 20th-century Chinese history, from civil wars to the Cultural Revolution.
- **Notability and Reception**: The film premiered at international festivals and received awards, including the Special Jury Prize at the Locarno Film Festival. Reviews highlight its stylistic innovation and historical insight, though some note its lengthy runtime as potentially challenging.
- **Production Context**: Directed by documentary filmmaker Qiu Jiongjiong in his fiction debut, the film draws from his family history, with his father portraying a key role based on the director's grandfather.
- **Release and Availability**: It screened at various festivals starting in 2021 and had limited theatrical releases, including in the US in 2022 and France in 2025.

### Background
The film explores themes of art, memory, and political upheaval through the lens of traditional Sichuan opera. Research suggests it avoids direct confrontation with sensitive historical events by using allegorical and theatrical framing, allowing for a nuanced portrayal of China's past.

### Critical Insights
Evidence from reviews leans toward positive assessments, with critics appreciating the film's ironic style and visual artistry. However, opinions vary on its accessibility, as the experimental approach may not appeal to all audiences.

*A New Old Play* (Chinese: 椒麻堂会; pinyin: Jiāo Má Táng Huì) is a 2021 drama film written and directed by Qiu Jiongjiong. The film depicts the life of Qiu Fu, a performer in Sichuan opera, whose experiences span major events in 20th-century Chinese history, including civil war, the Second Sino-Japanese War, the establishment of the People's Republic of China, and the Cultural Revolution. Presented through a blend of fictional narrative, historical reminiscence, and theatrical staging, it incorporates supernatural elements set in the underworld. 

Qiu Jiongjiong, previously known for documentary films, made his fiction feature debut with *A New Old Play*, drawing inspiration from his grandfather's career in opera. The film premiered in the international competition at the 74th Locarno Film Festival in August 2021, where it received the Special Jury Prize. It has been screened at numerous international film festivals and received limited theatrical releases in several countries. Critics have described it as an innovative work that uses artificial sets and ironic techniques to explore personal and collective memory, comparing it to films such as Hou Hsiao-hsien's *The Puppetmaster* (1993) and Chen Kaige's *Farewell My Concubine* (1993).

## Plot
In the 1980s, Qiu Fu (Yi Sicheng), a prominent clown-role actor in Sichuan opera, dies and embarks on a journey to the Ghost City, escorted by underworld officials. As he encounters old acquaintances and reviews his life before consuming the Forgetfulness Soup to erase his memories, flashbacks reveal his story.

The narrative begins in the 1920s in Sichuan Province during a period of civil unrest. A soldier and opera enthusiast named Pocky (Qiu Zhimin) founds the "New-New" Troupe and adopts a seven-year-old orphan, the young Qiu Fu (Chen Haoyu). The troupe performs amid shifting political powers, affiliating with the military under the Nationalist Party. During the Second Sino-Japanese War, the group contributes to resistance efforts against Japanese occupation.

After the war, an adult Qiu Fu rises as a star performer, but the troupe faces pressures from the emerging Communist Party. The establishment of the People's Republic in 1949 brings nationalization of theaters, followed by hardships during events such as the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, including famine, political persecution, and confinement. The film frames these events through theatrical tableaux and supernatural interludes, emphasizing the persistence of art amid adversity.

## Cast
- Yi Sicheng as Qiu Fu (adult), the central clown-role performer.
- Chen Haoyu as Qiu Fu (young).
- Guan Nan as Huafeng, a troupe member.
- Qiu Zhimin as Pocky, the troupe founder (based on the director's grandfather).
- Xue Xuchun as Chicken Foot, a troupe associate.
- Gu Tao as Crooky, another troupe member.

The cast includes non-professional actors, with Qiu Zhimin, the director's father, portraying Pocky.

## Production
### Development
Qiu Jiongjiong, born in 1977, is a Chinese artist and filmmaker known for experimental documentaries such as *Mr. Zhang Believes* (2015). *A New Old Play* marks his first fiction feature, inspired by his grandfather's experiences as a Sichuan opera actor. Qiu initiated his interest in opera through family traditions and incorporated elements of painting, shadow theater, and opera into the film. The script was developed to counter official historical narratives through personal and artistic perspectives.

The project received support from the Golden Horse Film Project Promotion in 2017, the Hubert Bals Fund in 2018, and a CNC cash award. It was co-produced by companies in Hong Kong and France.

### Filming
Principal photography used studio sets to create artificial, theatrical environments, emphasizing irony and non-literal depictions. Cinematography was handled by Feng Yuchao (credited as "Robbin"), with sound design by Wang Ran, music by Diao Lili, costumes by Bai Yun, and art direction by Lv Xin. The film's runtime is 179 minutes.

## Release
*A New Old Play* premiered at the 74th Locarno Film Festival on August 7, 2021, in the international competition section. It subsequently screened at festivals including the Busan International Film Festival (October 2021), Golden Apricot Yerevan International Film Festival (October 2021), Festival des 3 Continents (November 2021), Singapore International Film Festival (November 2021), International Film Festival of Kerala (February 2022), Göteborg Film Festival (January 2022), and International Film Festival Rotterdam (January 2022).

The film had a limited theatrical release in the United States on May 20, 2022, and became available for streaming on May 16, 2023. In France, it was distributed by Carlotta Films and released in theaters on June 11, 2025. Distribution rights were sold to entities in France, Japan, and Singapore in 2024.

## Reception
On IMDb, the film holds a rating of 7.6 out of 10 based on over 600 user votes. On review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes, it has received positive feedback from critics, though an aggregate score is not available due to a limited number of reviews. 

Richard Brody of *The New Yorker* described the film as dramatizing Chinese political history with "affecting intimacy and candid observation—and with archly ironic methods," noting its use of contrived sets and fantasy sequences to signal non-literal truth. Austin Considine of *The New York Times* called it "at once tragedy and farce," reviving old stories through new life. Dennis Schwartz awarded it an A-, praising its tension for fans of Chinese opera and politics. Sean Gilman positioned it between *The Puppetmaster* and *Farewell My Concubine* as a history seen through a performer's eyes. 

Other reviews highlighted its multilayered nature and empathetic sparkle amid themes of futility. Shelly Kraicer noted it as a "daring, brilliant independent feature from China." The film's length of nearly three hours has been mentioned as potentially daunting, though lively in execution.

### Synopsis

One evening in the 1980s, Qiu Fu, a leading clown-role actor in 20th-century Sichuan opera, is killed in an accident and must reluctantly set off for the Ghost City under escort of two underworld officials. Along the way, he meets old friends. As they recall the past, earthly scenes creep into the mists of the underworld.
Qiu Fu’s life in opera unfolds against the backdrop of a secular upheaval. The "New-New" Troupe in which he grows up and learns his trade is affiliated with the military. As power shifts, the troupe is cast loose to wander rootlessly through a broken world. Despite this unsettled destiny, shaped by war, famine and political turmoil, Qiu Fu becomes one of the finest clown-role performers in Sichuan opera. And yet, one day he finds himself clapped in a pigsty as a political revolution rages outside.

### QIU Jiongjiong

QIU Jiongjiong (born 1977) is an active contemporary artist and filmmaker in China. As an artist, his works have been exhibited all over the world (for a detailed curriculum vitae please see attached). As a filmmaker, his experiments with cinematic language and aesthetics in documentary film-making have earned him a reputation as one of China's most important independent directors. His experimental/documentary feature MR. ZHANG BELIEVES (2015), supported by a Sundance Post-Production Grant, premiered at the Locarno International Film Festival and has been screened internationally. JIAO MA TANG HUI (A NEW OLD PLAY) is his first fiction feature.

### Selected Reviews:

A playful and vital work, a sincere act of love for a land and a culture steeped in history, a hymn to the Dionysian spirit of art.

---- Eddie Bertozzi (Head of Pardi di domani Selection Committee, Locarno)

Qiu Jiongjiong tells this story with affecting intimacy and candid observation—and with archly ironic methods. The movie is filmed as theatrical tableaux, complete with blatantly contrived sets and supernatural fantasy sequences, which virtually shout at viewers not to take the depicted events as literal truth.

---- Richard Brody (The New Yorker)

Qiu has made a cleverly contained existential epic, an ode to the innate persistence of workers, artists, and people in the face of futility and poor fortune. It is a wonder the film carries it off with an empathetic sparkle—there must be some purpose to art, to life, after all.

---- Daniel Kasman (MUBI Notebook)

Following Qiu Yu, a clown in the Sichuan opera who is based on the director’s famous grandfather, we venture into a fantasy-like world full of political drama based on the reality of living in China between the 1930s and the 1980s. With his two humorous sidekicks, Qiu Yu tries to negotiate his entry into Hades whilst his departing soul looks back on his childhood, performances, family tragedies, and political affairs.

![Image 6: ANewOldPlay_01](https://www.3continents.com/wp-content/uploads/thumbs/fullscreen/a/anewoldplay_01-1600x900.jpg)

The work of the well-known painter, Qiu Jiongiiong, seems to be underpinned throughout by an unyielding documentary resolve. Before _A New Old Play_, his first fiction film, six other films reveal an art of portraiture that combines the intimacy of the subject with the history of China to unfold the story of individuals ravaged and overwhelmed by circumstance. The crazy ambition of _A New Old Play_ is to manufacture (and this word takes on many concrete forms on screen) a kind of story that counters official history. Spanning half a century, the film unfurls its detailed and paranoid vision like a roll, encompassing the tradition of Sichuan Opera (the filmmaker was initiated to this at a very early age by his actor-grandfather), painting, shadow theatre, and a family and collective story. As the actor-narrator rekindles his memories and negotiates his reincarnation at the Gates of Hell, the artifices of studio shooting are what construct a precious resistance to oblivion.**Jérôme Baron**

[### Wes Anderson China-Style](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt14864160/reviews/?featured=rw9188146&ref_=tt_ururv_c_1_hd)

Mythologies about the afterlife can get somewhat confusing. Some simply believe that you die and you either go "up" or "down," to heaven or to hell. Still others believe there is a sort of waiting room, a purgatory, or a place where you just take a number and wait your turn (like in Beetlejuice). I recommend the hilarious "Defending Your Life," an Albert Brooks film that explores the process in Judgment City whereby ones' future placement is determined.  
  
In China, Nieh-ching-t'ai is a place in the Underworld where souls must review their lives before a mirror until the Yama King makes his judgment. And that is precisely the context for this film, which at its open finds the famous actor Qiu Fu (Yi Sicheng) entering the Underworld. He is greeted by two demons, Oxhead and Horseface aka Oxey and Horsey from Fengdu, the capital of Hell. They will be accompanying him on his journey through the Nieh-ching-t'ai.  
  
Beginning in 1920, when Qui was just a child starting his training with the New-New Theatrical Troupe, the film takes us through Qui's life and experience in a series of tableaus depicting the characters and experiences of the day. The movie reminded me of a Wes Anderson film in style. Along the way 20th century Chinese history is explored, along with some commentary on that history.  
  
My Wes Anderson comment is as much about the humor as it is the visual style. Comedy abounds in A New Old Play. The film is beautifully composed and cinematographically gorgeous. This is a masterpiece of Chinese independent cinema that may make its way onto some critics must see lists in years to come. The director Qiu Jiongjiong, who found inspiration from his own grandfather who was an actor like the Qui in the film, said, "I have rejected any tedious speculation, or supercilious detachment, in favor of lively, unabashed good humor and fun. . . The Dionysian spirit, the vital force, the clown in each of us. . . Hovering between reality and fantasy." It was a pleasure watching all 180 minutes of A New Old Play, released by Kani, and available at Vinegar Syndrome.

**_“The brightest light in the Chinese independent cinema world at this moment.”_**—Cinema Scope

Co-presented by [Bay Area Chinese Culture Salon](https://baccs.org/)

QIU Jiongjiong’s visually magnificent new film is a unique hybrid of fiction, historical reminiscence, and experimental theatre. Its overview of China from the 1930s to the 1980s is filtered through Qiu Yu, a Sichuan opera ‘clown’ based on the director’s own famous grandfather. As Qiu Yu negotiates his entry into Hades with two comic sidekicks, his departing soul reviews his childhood, his performances, family tragedies, and political perils.

This film of unparalleled aesthetic and political courage takes place in modestly spectacular visual settings: Qiu, a famous artist, has handcrafted an exquisite miniature model village, a fantastical river landscape, a golden sun in the shape of a Buddha’s head. These images set the scene for a constantly shifting acting style that embraces absurdism, political melodrama, comic vaudeville, and ritual tableaux. We are offered memory as a re-lived collective experience, insistently comic in its mode, but expansively humane in its vision. —IFFR

A New Old Play
==============

By [Richard Brody](https://www.newyorker.com/contributors/richard-brody)

May 13, 2022

![Image 3: A still from "A New Old Play” by director Qiu Jiongjiong.](https://media.newyorker.com/photos/627d68c180a172d2c29527d0/master/w_1280%2Cc_limit/220523_r40409.jpg)

Photograph courtesy Icarus Films

In **“A New Old Play,”** the Chinese director Qiu Jiongjiong daringly and imaginatively dramatizes twentieth-century Chinese political history—despite ongoing censorship in China—through the epoch-spanning story of a small theatre company. The movie, which opens on May 20 at Anthology Film Archives, is based on the life of the director’s grandfather. It depicts the birth of the New-New Theatre and Opera School—in Sichuan Province, in the nineteen-twenties—as a by-product of civil war and the Nationalist Party’s victory. The troupe’s founder, a soldier and an operaphile called Pocky (Qiu Zhimin, the director’s father), welcomes a seven-year-old foundling named Qiu Fu (Chen Haoyu), who becomes his prize student. During the Second World War, the company joins the resistance to Japanese occupation. After the war, when the adult Qiu Fu (Yi Sicheng) emerges as a star, the theatre faces pressure from the Communist Party; in the sixties, the Cultural Revolution proves catastrophic. Qiu Jiongjiong tells this story with affecting intimacy and candid observation—and with archly ironic methods. The movie is filmed as theatrical tableaux, complete with blatantly contrived sets and supernatural fantasy sequences, which virtually shout at viewers not to take the depicted events as literal truth._(May 13.)_

Published in the print edition of the [May 23, 2022](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2022/05/23), issue.
